152-022.r: Correct: China type climate → rain throughout the year; tropical highlands → vertical zonation of climates. Wrong: equatorial regions have four seasons (mainly two); Mediterranean gets summer rain (winter rain).

152-023.r: Mediterranean regions → rainy winters, because in winter pressure belts shift and they lie in the Westerlies belt (A and R true, R explains A); summers dry under subtropical high.

152-025.r: NW Europe ports open all year → warm North Atlantic flow stops the sea freezing; SW winds also blow all year but are not the reason (R not explanation).
152-025.t: Westerlies explain the mild temperature and good rain of Western Europe, not the ice-free ports.

152-026.r: Western European type climate → west edges of continents in the Westerlies belt; rain in all months and seasons, winter slightly more than summer. Both statements correct (UPPSC key).

152-027.r: Low annual and daily temperature range + precipitation all year (50–250 cm) → Marine West Coast climate (NW Europe, west coast of North America, southern Chile, New Zealand).
hi: Marine West Coast climate (पश्चिमी यूरोपीय/समुद्री जलवायु)

152-028.r: Data with mild, nearly even temperature (average 12.8°C), rain mostly in winter and dry June–August (54.9 cm a year) → Mediterranean region.
152-028.h: Mediterranean = wet winter, dry summer; dashes in June–August rainfall give it away.

152-029.r: Climates linked to shifting of pressure belts → Mediterranean and Monsoon (not Equatorial or Western European); monsoon winds emerge from shifting pressure belts.

152-030.r: Zaire (DR Congo) to the Netherlands → Equatorial → Hot desert (Sahara) → Mediterranean → West European climate (code 1, 3, 2, 4).

152-031.r: World's wettest place → Mawsynram (Meghalaya), as per this book.
152-031.t: Don't pick Cherrapunji here; in this question the answer is Mawsynram.

152-032.r: Coldest place outside polar regions → Verkhoyansk, Siberia (record of 1933); world's lowest temperature → Vostok, Antarctica, 21 July 1983.

152-033.r: Hottest → Sahara; coldest → Antarctica; wettest → Cherrapunji; driest → Chile (code 4 3 2 1).

152-034.r: Occasional weak Indian monsoon → El Nino and Southern Oscillation (ENSO); El Nino = warm current off Peru coast; La Nina = opposite, cooling of eastern equatorial Pacific.

152-035.r: El Nino and La Nina are both Pacific Ocean events (not Indian Ocean); El Nino weakens India's SW monsoon, La Nina strengthens it. Both statements wrong.
152-035.t: La Nina does affect the monsoon: it activates it, while El Nino harms it.

152-037.r: El Nino → warm current off Peru coast (eastern Pacific), every three to seven years; it raises water temperature by 10°C but reduces plankton and fish. Only statement 1 correct.
152-037.t: El Nino lowers plankton, not raises it.

152-039.r: Southern Oscillation → seesaw of air pressure, Tahiti (central Pacific) vs Port Darwin (Australia); with El Nino called ENSO.
152-039.c: The book gives no single answer (*): it argues (d) (Pacific only) but accepts (b) Pacific and Indian Ocean, the commission's answer.

152-040.r: El Nino and La Nina are climate patterns, not storms (incorrect statement). La Nina → stronger trade winds; El Nino → upwelling slows, fewer phytoplankton off the coast.

152-041.r: Data with cool, even temperatures and rain in every month, less in summer than winter → Western European type climate (Northern Hemisphere).

152-042.r: Data with hot summer (27.8°C), cold winter and rain all year, more in summer → China type climate.

152-043.r: Graph: temperature 15–25°C, heaviest rain in April, May, June (under 25 cm) → wet and dry tropical climate.

152-044.r: Hekistotherms → plants of very low temperature areas (tundra, mountains, Alpine forests).

152-045.r: 'Vegetation is the true index of climate' → Koppen (classification 1884; revised 1918, 1931, 1936), based on Candoll's five vegetation zones (1874).

152-046.r: No Mediterranean climate in the Pampas (temperate South American lowlands: Argentina, Uruguay); Central Chile, Cape Town and Adelaide have it.

153-001.r: Correct order of agricultural practices → Soil preparation → Sowing → Irrigation → Harvesting.

153-002.r: Water holding capacity (decreasing): Clay > Silt > Sand.
153-002.h: Finer the particle, more water it holds.

153-003.r: Capillary action is most effective in clayey soil (smallest pores): Clay > Silt > Loamy > Sandy.

153-004.r: Soil conservation → protecting soil from harm: control erosion and keep land highly fertile (better land use).

153-005.r: Terra rossa → red clay soil formed by weathering of limestone and dolomite rocks.

153-006.r: Soil leaching → major problem in tropical rainforests, due to heavy rain throughout the year.

153-007.r: Halophytes → saline soils; cryophytes → cold soil; lithophytes → rocks; xerophytes → deserts; hygrophytes → waterlogged areas; hydrophytes → water.

153-008.r: Nitrogen is added to soil by excretion of urea by animals and death of vegetation (decomposition, nitrogen cycle); not by burning coal.

153-009.r: Clay holds maximum water (A true) because its particles are small; its pores are small, not large (R false).
153-009.c: The book prints (c) (both correct), but its own explanation says R is wrong; by that, (b) is the right answer.

153-010.r: Contour bunding → used on mountain/hill slopes to slow rain runoff and check erosion; not desert margins, flood plains or scrublands → None of the above.

153-011.r: Podzol → cold temperate; Chernozem → temperate cold steppe; Spodosols → humid cold temperate; Laterite → hot and humid.

153-012.r: Earthworms are good for agriculture (A false): 'ecosystem engineers' that make pores, break soil into fine soft particles and act as decomposers (R true).

153-013.r: Only 3 true: irrigation over time can salinise farmland. Wrong: organic matter raises (not reduces) water holding capacity; soil does play a role in the sulphur cycle.

153-014.r: Edaphic factor → soil (its physical and chemical make-up); climatic, biotic and topographic are other factors.

153-015.r: Oldest to latest: Sihawal (Lower Paleolithic) → Patpara (Middle Paleolithic) → Baghor (Upper Paleolithic) → Khetaurhi (Neolithic, Microlithic); code 4, 1, 3, 2.

153-016.r: Geographical cycle of erosion → W.M. Davis; Walter Penck rejected it (morphological system); Holmes → convection currents; Kober → geosynclinal orogen theory.

154-001.r: Nomadic herding → mostly in dry (arid) areas: steppes of Eurasia, Central Asia, Africa, South America.

154-002.r: Transhumance → seasonal movement of people and herds between valley/lowland and mountain pastures; in India, Himalayan Bhotiya, Bakarwal and Gaddi practise it.

154-003.r: Most recent → Cro-Magnon humans: early Homo sapiens, about 40,000 to 10000 years ago; first remains found 1868, Dordogne, France.
154-003.t: Heidelberg and Neanderthal humans are older.

154-004.r: First bird → Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years ago.

154-006.r: Afrikaners → white minority of South Africa, from Dutch, German and French (Huguenot) settlers; speak Afrikaans, which grew from Dutch.

154-007.r: Largest racial group → Caucasoid (skull index over 80; Nordic, Alpine, Mediterranean types).

154-008.r: Jews → Israel; Teda → Libya; Beja → Egypt; Lur → Iran (code 4 3 1 2).

154-009.r: Original home of the Gypsies → India; believed to come from the 'Dom' caste.

154-010.r: Pygmies → equatorial rainforest of the Congo River basin, Africa; hunter-gatherers living in leaf-and-branch huts called mongulus.

154-013.r: Pygmy house type → hut built in a tree, reached by a ladder (picture option a).

154-014.r: Not pastoral nomads → Pygmies (hunter-gatherers of Congo Basin); Kazaks, Masai and Lapps are pastoral nomads.

154-015.r: Eskimo → Canada (also Alaska, Greenland, N Russia; Inuit and Yupik groups). Oraon and Gonds → India (Oraon: Chotanagpur); Lapps → European tundra.

154-016.r: Bushman → Kalahari Desert (correct pair). Eskimo → Canada, Alaska, Greenland; Pygmy → Central Africa; Bundu → Western Africa.

154-017.r: Eskimo → Canada (and Greenland); Maasai → Kenya; Bedouins → Saudi Arabia; Bushman → Botswana (Kalahari).

154-019.r: Khirghiz → Central Asia; Bushman → Kalahari; Ainu → Japan; Bedouin → Arab (code 3 4 1 2).

154-020.r: Kayak → narrow hunting boat; Umiak → boat for transport; Sledge → dog-pulled vehicle; Inuit (Eskimos) → snow house (igloo).
154-020.t: Kayak is the narrow hunting boat; Umiak is the bigger transport boat.

154-021.r: Bushman → Namibia; Bedouins → Saudi Arabia; Pygmies → Congo; Maasai → Kenya (code 2 3 1 4).

154-022.r: Wrong pair: Masai – West Africa; Masai live in East Africa. Correct: Bushman – Kalahari; Eskimo – Northern Canada; Pygmy – Congo Basin.

154-023.r: Semang tribe → forests of the Malay Peninsula (Malaysia); Negrito race.

154-024.r: Wrong pair: Semangs – Indonesia; Semang belong to Malaysia. Correct: Berber – Morocco; Inuits – Canada; Veddas – Sri Lanka.

154-025.r: Zulu → South Africa; battle of Isandlwana, British vs Zulus, 1879.

154-026.r: Bushmen → Kalahari Desert, most in Botswana; Ainu – Japan, Maasai – Kenya, Papuans – New Guinea are correct.
154-026.c: The book gives no single answer (*): all pairs can pass, but it takes (b) Bushmen – Union of South Africa as the wrong one.

154-028.r: Bushmen → Botswana (also Namibia, South Africa, Angola); hunter-gatherers of Southern Africa.

154-029.r: Wrong pair: Congo basin – Negrito; Congo basin → Pygmy, Negrito → Southeast Asia. Correct: Alpine – Central Asia; Kalahari – Bushmen; Scandinavia – Nordic.

154-030.r: Wrong pair: Maasai – Western Africa; Maasai are pastoral nomads of East Africa (Kenya, northern Tanzania, eastern Uganda).

154-031.r: Wrong pair: Maasai – Zambia; Maasai → Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda. Correct: Maori – New Zealand; Mayas – Guatemala; Bushman – Kalahari.

154-032.r: Kurds live in Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, all formed from the former Soviet Union.
154-032.c: The book gives no single answer (*): it says all four options have Kurdish people.

154-033.r: Inuit → Arctic regions of Greenland (Denmark), Canada, Russia and Alaska; not Sweden.

154-034.r: Wrong pair: Bantu – Sahara; Bantu → East, Central and Southern Africa. Correct: Fulani – West Africa; Masai – East Africa; Nuba – Sudan.

154-035.r: Lapps (Sami) → Scandinavia: Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula (Fenno-Scandinavian region).

154-036.r: Natives of North America → Mongoloid racial group.

154-037.r: Wrong pair: Khirghiz – Sudan; Khirghiz live in Central Asia. Correct: Pygmy – Congo basin; Angami – Nagaland; Ainu – Japan.

154-038.r: All pairs correct → (e): Masai – Central Eastern Africa; Sakai – Malaysia (and Indonesia); Bedouin – Arabian Peninsula; Kirghiz – Central Asia.

154-039.r: Wrong pair: Alaska – Koryak; Koryak are a tribe of Russia (some in Ukraine). Correct: Borneo – Punan; Arab Desert – Ruwala; Sweden and Finland – Lapps.

154-040.r: Keystone species → species that decide whether many other species can persist in a community.

154-041.r: China, Mongolia, Japan → Mongoloid race; Australoid → Melanesia, Australia; Negroid → Africa; Nordic → northern and north-western Europe.

155-001.r: Esperanto → artificial international auxiliary language meant to serve as a world language; devised by Dr. Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof.

155-002.r: Most speakers when asked → Mandarin (Chinese); counting L1 (mother tongue) + L2 (second language), English is now spoken by the most people.

155-004.r: Spanish is official in Chile, Colombia and Cuba; not in the Republic of Congo.

155-005.r: Tamil → official language of Singapore (with Malay, English, Mandarin); Myanmar → Burmese; Indonesia → Indonesian; Mauritius → English, French.

155-006.r: Map of the Americas: 1 → French (French Guiana); 2 → Portuguese (Brazil); 3 → Spanish (Argentina); 4 → English.

155-007.r: Pakistan has more ethnic diversity than Bangladesh (A true); Pakistan's official languages → English and Urdu; Punjabi is most spoken but not official (R false).

155-008.r: Wrong pair: Bahasa – Thailand; Bahasa → Indonesia. Correct: Danish – Denmark; Dutch – Netherlands; Mandarin – China.

156-001.r: Leading producer of both wheat and rice when asked → China. FAO 2024: wheat → China, India, Russia, USA; rice → India, China, Bangladesh, Indonesia.

156-002.r: Rice production → India ranks first in the world (FAO 2024).

156-003.r: Largest area under rice cultivation → India, then China (FAO 2024); Japan and Philippines far behind.

156-004.r: Wheat production, descending (FAO 2024): China > India > Russia > USA (option a); when asked, USA was third (option b).

156-005.r: Largest wheat producer in the world → China (FAO 2024).

156-006.r: Highest rice productivity when asked → China. FAO 2024: Tajikistan tops (13385.8 kg/ha), then Australia; China 7149.5, Japan 6956.1, India 4313.2 kg/ha.

156-007.r: Hybrid rice → most popular in China (on more than half its rice land).

156-008.r: World's Rice Gene Bank → International Rice Research Institute, Los Banos, Philippines.

156-009.r: Rice share of total exports (FAO 2013): Thailand 14.09%, Myanmar 11.79%, Japan 0.60%, Indonesia 0.00%; commission chose Myanmar.
156-009.c: No option earns two-thirds of its exports from rice (the commission took (c) Myanmar). Also note: India, not Cambodia or the USA, is the world's largest rice exporter by quantity and value.

156-010.r: Largest sugarcane producer → Brazil, then India, China, Pakistan (FAO 2024).

156-011.r: Second largest sugarcane producer → India, after Brazil (FAO 2024).

156-012.r: Two largest sugar beet producers → France and Russia (when asked); FAO 2024 → Russia and Germany.

156-013.r: Ukraine → makes almost all its sugar from sugar beet only.

156-014.r: Largest cotton producer among options when asked → USA (after China). FAO 2023: India is the largest cottonseed producer, then China, Brazil, USA, Pakistan.

156-015.r: Highest cotton yield per hectare (2014) among options → Australia. FAO 2024: China first (6588.5 kg/ha), then Australia, Turkiye.

156-016.r: Highest cotton yield among USA, China, Pakistan, India → China (6588.5 kg/ha, FAO 2024).

156-017.r: Castor oilseeds → India was the largest producer and exporter when asked; the book cites FAO 2024 naming Ethiopia as largest exporter.

156-018.r: Largest banana producer → India (37.61 million tonnes, FAO 2024), then China, Indonesia, Ecuador, Brazil.

156-019.r: Largest coconut producer → Indonesia, then India, Philippines (FAO 2024).

156-020.r: Coconut and sugarcane farming in the Philippines → developed by the Spanish and Americans.

156-021.r: India → second-largest fruit producer in the world, after China; first only in FAO's 'other fruits n.e.c.' group (FAOSTAT 2024).
156-021.c: India is the world's second-largest fruit producer after China, so (d) Second is the standard answer; the book's 'first' uses only FAO's 'other fruits n.e.c.' group.

156-022.r: Largest tobacco producer → China (2.26 million tonnes), then India, Brazil (FAO 2024).

156-023.r: Correct when asked: China → largest tobacco producer; India → largest jowar producer. Wrong: soybean (USA then, Brazil now); raw silk led by China, not Italy.
156-023.t: Now (FAO 2024) USA leads sorghum (jowar), then Nigeria and India.

156-024.r: Mauritius → exports the highest share of its sugar output; its economy rests on sugar exports and tourism.

156-025.r: Largest natural rubber producer → Thailand, then Indonesia, Cote d'Ivoire, Vietnam, China (FAO 2024).

156-026.r: Two major natural rubber producers → Thailand and Indonesia (FAO 2024).

156-027.r: About one-third of world natural rubber → Thailand (FAO 2024).

156-028.r: Largest rubber cultivation among the options when asked → India; FAO 2024: Thailand, Indonesia and Cote d'Ivoire lead.

156-029.r: Sri Lanka gave up coffee → leaf rust (fungus Hemileia vastatrix); the epidemic began in Sri Lanka in 1869 and hit British colonies from the 1860s.

156-030.r: Two leading coffee producers → Brazil and Vietnam; then Colombia, Indonesia, Ethiopia, Uganda, India (FAO 2024).

156-031.r: Highest coffee producer → Brazil, then Vietnam, Colombia (FAO 2023).

156-032.r: Top share of world coffee production → Brazil (FAO 2024).

156-033.r: Second largest coffee exporter → Vietnam, after Brazil (FAO 2024, by quantity).

156-034.r: Robusta → coffee variety (Coffea canephora), native to Central and Western sub-Saharan Africa (Ethiopia, Uganda); also grown in India.

156-035.r: Largest tea exporter when asked (FAO 2004) → Sri Lanka; FAO 2024 → Kenya by quantity, China by value.

156-036.r: Largest tea exporter when asked (2015) → China; FAO 2024 → Kenya by quantity, China by value.
156-036.t: Kenya leads tea exports by quantity, China by value.

156-037.r: Largest tea exporter by value in 2016-17 → China (also in 2024); India 4th by value (2024).

156-038.r: Coffee → Sao Paulo Plateau; Jute → Ganges delta; Rice → Yangtze plains; Wheat → Prairies plains (code 3 4 2 1).

156-039.r: Coffee → Sao Paulo; Rice → Yangzi Jiang basin; Wheat → Huang He basin (winter wheat); Tea → Candy (Kandy) basin, Sri Lanka (code 2 1 4 3).

156-040.r: Cocoa → Ghana; Coffee → Ivory Coast; Tea → Kenya; Sugarcane → South Africa (code 4 1 2 3).

156-041.r: Coffee-growing US state → Hawaii (famous Kona coffee).

156-042.r: Not tropical → Apple: grown in temperate and subtropical regions, as its flowering needs cold conditions.
156-042.c: Walnut is also a temperate, not tropical, fruit, so option (a) fits too; the book's answer is Apple.

156-043.r: Large labour on small holdings → commercial horticulture (fruits, vegetables, flowers; also tea, coffee, sugarcane, rubber), as crops need continuous supervision.

156-044.r: Rubber → Malaysia; Coffee → Colombia; Olive → Italy; Sugarcane → Mauritius (code 4 3 2 1).

156-045.r: China → iron ore; India → milk; Saudi Arabia → petroleum (now USA, 2023); Thailand → natural rubber (code 3 2 4 1).

156-046.r: Tropical plantations → bunched along sea coasts (true); Amazon Basin suits rubber but lacks workers (true); not mainly lowlands, they need well-drained hill slopes (false).

156-047.r: Plantation crops → coffee, rubber, coconut and spices are all plantation crops (with tea, cocoa, arecanut, cashew), per Agriculture and Commerce Ministries.
156-047.c: No option lists all four. By the Commerce Ministry's list (tea, coffee, rubber, spices), (d) 1, 2 and 4 fits; coconut counts as a plantation crop only under the Agriculture Ministry.

156-048.r: Crops grown in alleys between rows of planted trees → alley cropping; intercropping is the wider term (includes relay, mixed and alley cropping).

156-049.r: Monoculture → distinct feature of commercial grain farming.

156-050.r: Not shifting cultivation → Fazenda (plantations of Brazil); Chena, Jhooming and Milpa are types of shifting cultivation.

156-051.r: Taungya → villagers grow farm crops in the early stage of a forest plantation; mainly in Myanmar.

156-052.r: Ladang → shifting agriculture; local name used mainly in Malaysia and Indonesia.

156-053.r: Correct: Jhumming → South-East Asia; Milpa → Mexico and Central America. Wrong: Ladang → Indonesia, not Sri Lanka. All are slash-and-burn farming.

156-054.r: Nitrogen deficiency → stunted growth, pale green-yellow leaves (less chlorophyll), because nitrogen drives green leaf growth (A and R true, R explains A).

156-055.r: Only Nostoc → biofertilizer: a blue-green alga (cyanobacteria, like Anabaena) that fixes atmospheric nitrogen for paddy; Agaricus and Spirogyra are not.

156-056.r: Azolla-Anabaena biofertilizer → used for rice; Azolla itself is a biofertilizer.

156-058.r: Blue-green algae biofertilizer → boosts rice (paddy) production.

156-059.r: Alfalfa (Medicago sativa) → a kind of grass, native to Asia; rich in vitamins A, C, E, K, B and minerals.

156-060.r: Africa has tea (A false): first grown at Durban Botanical Garden, 1850; Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda are major producers. Tea needs fertile, humus-rich soil (R true).
